claims.text: Controlled cryogenic pre-straining of a refractory high-entropy alloy will induce a high density of nano-twins.
Nano-twins act as barriers to dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
Nano-twinning provides an additional plastic-deformation mode that can improve ductility.
Cryogenic pre-straining will simultaneously improve yield strength and ductility relative to conventional processing.
A solution-treated BCC refractory high-entropy alloy may show brittle behavior.
A solution-treated FCC refractory high-entropy alloy may have limited strength.
Approximately 5–10% plastic pre-strain at about 77 K can initiate nano-twin formation without causing premature fracture.
Refractory HEAs with moderate stacking-fault energies can support deformation twinning.
The proposed cryogenic treatment is applicable to certain FCC or dual-phase refractory HEAs.
The cryogenic pre-straining treatment will produce nano-twins distributed uniformly throughout the microstructure.
Multiple twin orientations provide additional pathways for plastic deformation through twinning-induced plasticity.
The combined strengthening and deformation effects of nano-twins can overcome the conventional strength–ductility trade-off.
After cryogenic pre-straining, the alloy will have higher room-temperature yield strength than the untreated alloy.
After cryogenic pre-straining, the alloy will have greater room-temperature uniform elongation than the untreated alloy.
Alloys with microstructures and stacking-fault energies that do not favor twinning may not benefit from the treatment.
Highly brittle alloys or alloys that form detrimental phases during deformation may not show the proposed improvement.
The magnitude of improvement will vary with composition, pre-strain level, and processing conditions.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant increase in both yield strength and uniform ductility relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mediator requires retention of deformation-induced nano-twins, but the experiment proposes homogenizing samples after pre-straining. A post-strain homogenization treatment could anneal out the twins and pre-strain dislocation structure, removing the intended mediator before testing.

The main hypothesis is phrased broadly for refractory HEAs, whereas the conditions and boundary restrict it to the narrower subset with twinning-favorable stacking-fault energy and FCC or dual-phase characteristics.
